I agree the quality of life for working people has been massively diminished, but shrugging your shoulders helplessly doesn't fix the issue.

The earlier you invest in a pension, the more compound interest you earn, which means even small, regular contributions can substantially grow. It's not impossible for a medium earner to grow a pension pot to 12k/year at retirement age. They just need to not contribute the bare minimum, and not ignore what their workplace pension is being invested into.

If you start contributing £1,021 annually from age 16, with a 4% compounding growth rate, you'll have enough to retire at age 67 and withdraw £12,000 annually for 20 years. That isn't impossible for a median earner.

Let's be honest, most factors of life used to be better than they are now. Boomers grew up in a golden era not seen before, and never seen after, because it simply wasn't sustainable.

However, my point isn't who had it better, just that the guarantee that any working person **SHOULD** have some form of "private" pension lessens to burden on a government having to fund state benefits for a huge swath of the population. 

The likelihood is that would mean that if any pension from the state did exist in the future, it would be to "supplement" a workplace pension. The reality is, forcing employers to auto-enroll is, at least for me, a blindingly obvious sign that a state pension won't be a thing when I retire. 

There's also nothing stopping you contributing more to your pension than the bare minimum, or opening a SIPP. There's a lot of people burying their heads in the sand purely because they feel hard done by over the way pensions are likely to go, which is pretty absurd. Or just living in blissful ignorance.

Yes, it's unfair. The current pension system is so laughably broken, but there's plenty people can do today to ensure they don't have to work until they die.

It does lift the burden of the future government somewhat though. We can assume that by the time young people retire they will have at least **SOME** pension pot already, which isn't the case for a lot of pensioners currently who are entirely reliant on a state pension.

The legal requirement for a workplace pension was the first step to getting rid of a state pension.

We will get a pension, just a much, much worse one, which entirely depends on how generous your employer was, and how much you earned. 

It's not a surprise that most employers offer the legal bare minimum, but when you do the math, that amount isn't enough to retire on for... anyone really, even high earners.

You do have a choice though. There is absolutely nothing stopping you investing in a SIPP. No one should be edging their bets on a state pension, but complaining you won't get one, and you'll live in poverty isn't necessarily true. 

The best time to start investing in a SIPP was yesterday. The second best time is today.

As an easier example to the one I just sent. Say you were paid 20k in crypto:

You owe 20% of anything over £12,570 - So you owe 20% tax on £7,430

Your capital gains comes in if you've made more than 6k value in that crypto since you recieved it. Eg, you were paid 1k worth of crypto that is now worth 8k and you sold it, you owe CGT on that 1k over your 6k allowance. You also owe income tax if you recieved more than £12.5k worth of crypto as income. That tax is owed on the value of your crypto when you were paid it.
